scope: Reviewed background prose and five approved reference release-year corrections. Reference membership, order, IDs, titles and artists are unchanged; user library data is never modified.
method: Compared all supplied old texts with the bundled notes; reviewed wording and added claims against the cited English Wikipedia articles, with selected primary-source checks. This is an editorial source-alignment review, not an independent verification of every historical claim. The eight held proposals were subsequently researched and approved, using English or explicitly reviewed French Wikipedia adaptations and documented disc, label, library, chart and award sources. Conflicting edition dates and source limitations are recorded in the resolutions.

It was recorded in August 1988 at the Power Station in New York City by Zorn and Tim Berne on alto saxophones, Mark Dresser on bass, and Joey Baron and Michael Vatcher on drums. The album approaches free jazz from the perspective of hardcore punk, particularly taking note of the contemporary innovations of thrashcore and grindcore, and its liner notes thank figures from that scene such as Mick Harris of Napalm Death. Zorn would later pursue these preoccupations in the thrash jazz group Naked City. Like classic free jazz albums such as Free Jazz and Ascension, it has different saxophonists improvising simultaneously in stereo, with Berne on the left channel and Zorn on the right.

An R&B and pop record with dance, funk and hip hop elements, its lyrics explore independence, self-esteem, romance and relationships between women. Four singles were released: "Survivor", "Bootylicious", a cover of Samantha Sang's "Emotion", and "Nasty Girl". The album debuted at number one on the Billboard 200 with first-week sales of 663,000 copies, the group's only number-one studio album there. The title track won the Grammy Award for Best R&B Performance by a Duo or Group with Vocals, and the album was nominated for Best R&B Album. Survivor was certified quadruple platinum by the RIAA and had sold over 10 million copies worldwide by 2004.
